items.title: The Indian 'Tamasha queen' whose fans paid for a show that never happened
items.summary: A new Bollywood flim spotlights the remarkable life of dancer and singer Vithabhai Narayangaonkar.
items.body:
Image source, Pradnya Daya Pawar

Image caption,

Vithabhai Narayangaonkar was a legend in Maharashtra's folk theatre

ByAmrita Kadam, BBC Marathi and Zoya Mateen, BBC News, Delhi

Few things could keep Vithabai Narayangaonkar, one of the greatest stars of Maharashtra's folk theatre, away from the stage.

Not even, it would seem, the birth of her child.

In the 1960s, the singer, dancer and troupe leader was performing in Shikhar Shingnapur, a village in the western Indian state, when she went into labour.

"She quietly stepped behind the stage into a makeshift tent while the rest of us continued performing," her daughter, veteran folk artist Mangala Bansode, told BBC Marathi.

Outside, the restless audience kept shouting: "Where is Vitha?"

When Vithabai returned to the stage, she was cradling her newborn son, the seventh of her eight children.

"The audience was stunned, but they quietly left, saying, 'We will watch your performance later'," Bansode recalled.

Outspoken and quick-witted, Vithabai held audiences across Maharashtra in thrall for decades, earning the title of Tamasha Samradnyi – the empress of Tamasha, the state's traditional travelling folk theatre.

Now, more than two decades after her death, her life has inspired a Bollywood musical, Eetha, starring Shraddha Kapoor, and due for release on 4 December.

Directed by Laxman Utekar, Eetha is based on Yogiraj Bagul's Marathi book chronicling Vithabai's life.

Rooted in devotional poetry, Tamasha evolved into a lively mix of music, dance, comedy and drama. At its heart is Lavani, a song and dance tradition in which verses ranging from the bawdy to the politically incisive are performed to the beat of the dholki, a percussion instrument.

Eetha evokes the world of Tamasha in its heyday. Kapoor, who had never performed Lavani before, learnt to dance while wearing musical anklets weighing 4kg each.

"The lives of Tamasha artists have been very tough, so in their dance you see pain as well as joy," Kapoor recalled at a promotional event.

Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

Eetha hits the theatres on 5 December

Many Tamasha performers, including Vithabai, came from oppressed castes, facing discrimination even as their artistry drew large crowds.

How much of that history Eetha will capture remains debated. Utekar says it is not a biopic, but his decision to rename the protagonist Vithabai Bhau Gavkar instead of Vithabai Bhau Mang Narayangaonkar has drawn criticism.

For critics, much of Vithabai's history was contained in her name – Mang identified her with a historically oppressed Dalit community, while Narayangaonkar spoke of her family's roots in Narayangaon village. Both featured in the name of the troupe she inherited from her father – Bhau-Bapu Mang Narayangaonkar Tamasha Mandal.

Vithabai spoke openly about caste and the indignities Tamasha artists faced, themes that also surfaced in her songs. In a 1960s Lavani documented by historian Shailaja Paik, she rebuked men for lewd gestures, reminding them she danced to earn a living, not to please them.

It was a livelihood she had inherited from generations of performers in her family.

Like her son, Vithabai was born during a Tamasha performance, in 1935. Her mother, Shanta, had continued touring with her husband Bhau's troupe throughout her pregnancy.

Vithabai joined a theatre group at eight and her father's troupe at 13, soon becoming its star. After her father and co-leader Bapu died in quick succession, she took over the troupe with her husband and cousin.

Her career flourished during Tamasha's golden age, when productions grew more elaborate, drawing on mythology, history and contemporary life, says folk arts scholar Sukhada Khandge.

Khandge, who watched Vithabai perform as a child, recalls her sparkling eyes and commanding presence. She was as expressive with her face as she was with her feet.

Image source, Pradnya Daya Pawar

Image caption,

Vithabai was known as the empress of Tamasha in Maharashtra

Her fame carried her beyond Maharashtra.

During India's war with China in 1962, Vithabai performed for soldiers in the North-East Frontier Agency, now largely Arunachal Pradesh, braving freezing conditions just three months after giving birth, Bansode says.

At a conference in 1996, she recalled meeting soldiers from the historically oppressed Mahar and Mang communities at the frontier.

"Our Mahar-Mang soldiers were expected to fight and lay down their lives defending the nation, but the very same people would not even allow our bridegroom to pass through the village entrance," she said.

Despite offers from leading filmmakers, including Raj Kapoor, and roles in Marathi cinema, Vithabai refused to leave theatre. Film fame, she felt, would benefit her alone, while her troupe supported some 50 families, Bansode says.

There was a tenderness, too, in her relationship with audiences.

In his book on Vithabai's life, which inspired Eetha, Yogiraj Bagul recounts a performance in Mumbai during Diwali in 1971.

Despite the threat of rain, spectators insisted on buying tickets, saying the money would be their Bhau Beej gift to Vithabai if the show was cancelled – a festival celebrating the bond between brothers and sisters.

When the rain came, people left chanting: "Bhau Beej, Bhau Beej."

No one asked for their money back.

But Vithabai's fortunes failed to match her fame. Her husband, Maruti Sawant, mismanaged the troupe's finances and took loans in her name, family members say. By the time she left him in 1982, she was heavily indebted.

Bagul also writes about a 1986 column in a Marathi daily that revealed how the empress of Tamasha was now travelling on public buses and staying in cheap accommodation.

Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

Despite drawing huge crowds, Lavni dancers were often disdained

Despite public support, Vithabai was forced to disband her troupe in 1990 – the same year she received the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award, one of India's highest performing arts honours.

Vithabai successfully campaigned for government pensions for Tamasha artists. But many of the hardships she knew persist today, says Marathi writer Pradnya Daya Pawar.

Troupes spend nearly eight months a year on the road, with performers struggling to feed their children and educate them, she says. Despite government aid, many remain indebted to private moneylenders.

Vithabai's financial struggles persisted until her death in January 2002. Her family could pay only 4,000 of the 5,900 rupees owed to the Pune hospital where she died, the Times of India reported.

Fellow artists and admirers chipped in to bring her body home to Narayangaon.

Maharashtra has since instituted a lifetime achievement award in her name.

Eetha could now introduce Vithabai to a generation that never saw her perform, though the changes to her name have left some uneasy.

Marathi writer Pragya Daya Pawar argues that omitting the reference to Vithabai's caste risks obscuring the difficulties she confronted.

"It erases the social location, struggle and resistance that shaped her remarkable journey, reducing an extraordinary artist's story to a purely individual achievement," she says.

But Bansode, who spent years performing alongside her mother, says there is much to celebrate.

"The name doesn't matter to me. I am simply proud that a film is being made about my mother," she says.

items.title: A clinic is offering to reassess ADHD and autism diagnoses - and hundreds of people are interested
items.summary: While many people find a diagnosis for ADHD or autism affirming, a government-funded clinic in Sweden is re-assessing people who feel it does not reflect them.
items.body:
Image source, BBC / WOODY MORRIS

Image caption,

Johanna, 24, began questioning her ADHD diagnosis when she discovered it could act as a barrier to becoming a police officer

ByKate Bowie

Global Health

Freya looks nervous as she walks into a psychiatric clinic in Sweden for an ADHD assessment.

Countries around the world have seen a huge increase in ADHD diagnoses over recent decades. For many people this can be life changing, helping them understand themselves better and access support.

But Freya (not her real name) is not attending a long-awaited appointment to secure a diagnosis.

This government-funded clinic offers autism and ADHD diagnosis reassessments - its doctors believe it is the first in the world dedicated solely to this purpose.

At 12, Freya was struggling with anxiety at school and sought out professional help. "They thought I had ADHD," she says.

But as she grew up, she felt that she did not experience ADHD symptoms. "I don't think I had it in the first place," she now says.

Her doubts about the diagnosis became more pressing as a teenager, when she discovered that in Sweden, it could be a barrier to pursuing her dream career of joining the police.

"I want to have every option open," she tells BBC World Service.

If the doctors at the clinic decide Freya does not meet the ADHD criteria, her medical records will be updated, and it will be easier for her to apply for a job with the police.

The clinic, known as Mottagning Neuropsykiatri, has opened at a time when rates of ADHD and autism diagnoses are under the spotlight. Many say this is because of greater awareness of the symptoms, and that previously neglected groups - particularly women and girls - are finally getting the diagnoses they need, while others argue that the growing numbers stem from overdiagnosis.

The existence of the clinic is controversial. Clinical guidance from UK governing bodies and the World Health Organization describe autism as a lifelong condition and ADHD as a neurodevelopmental condition that can persist into adulthood. The medical consensus is that both diagnoses last a lifetime, even if symptoms fluctuate.

And some neurodiversity advocates warn that a dedicated reassessment service could reinforce the idea that being diagnosed with ADHD or autism is undesirable – and deepen the stigma surrounding both conditions.

Despite this, hundreds of people have approached the clinic about reassessment.

Image source, BBC / WOODY MORRIS

Image caption,

Psychologist Sebastian Lundström runs the clinic, which operates one day a month

Barred from jobs

Like Freya, other young adults have been prompted to reconsider their diagnosis after they felt it had become a barrier.

This is because historically, Swedes with ADHD or autism were barred from certain jobs, including joining the military, and becoming police officers, train drivers and pilots. This is despite research suggesting some neurodivergent traits can be strengths in certain roles. No such bans exist in the UK, although rules differ globally.

Since 2022, people with ADHD have been able to join the Swedish military if they are medication-free. And since 2021, people with ADHD or autism have been able to apply to join the police, but must submit a medical certificate, which can cost around 15,000 SEK (£1,100) privately.

When Freya was referred to the clinic, she says she was relieved to find out she could get her diagnosis reassessed there for free.

Johanna, 24, was diagnosed with ADHD at 14 after what she describes as a period of bad behaviour at school. She found the diagnosis helpful at first and received additional support from teachers.

But as she grew into adulthood, she says she stopped feeling that she needed extra support. And after discovering it was a barrier to becoming a police officer, she began questioning whether it was even accurate.

Johanna says she has some traits of ADHD, such as a short attention span, "but not enough to have an ADHD diagnosis," she believes.

Johanna was reassessed aged 21 during an early pilot of the reassessment clinic and was found not to meet its diagnostic criteria for ADHD. She now works for her father's company, and does not plan on becoming a police officer.

What is an ADHD or autism reassessment?

Both ADHD and autism are neurodevelopmental conditions that affect how people think and interact with the world. They are diagnosed through detailed assessments, which can include questionnaires and interviews, rather than one single clinical test.

The doctors at Mottagning Neuropsykiatri say their approach is different from traditional assessments, as it focuses less on someone's history, and more on the symptoms they are experiencing in the present.

"This is not de-diagnosing, this is a renewed assessment of your functioning today," says Sebastian Lundström, the clinic's lead psychologist.

The doctors say they do not judge whether the original assessment was correct, so rather than wiping the original diagnosis from patients' medical records, they add a note of the new assessment.

Lundström says that some people who once had a diagnosis but are found to not meet the criteria at the clinic may have been misdiagnosed. But he also believes that for a small minority, ADHD and autism are not lifelong conditions and individuals may stop experiencing symptoms as they grow older.

But updating a person's diagnosis because they are not currently showing symptoms is a contested approach.

"We have to remember that these are lifelong conditions," says Navid Ghannad, chair of Autism Skåne, a local Swedish non-profit for autistic people and their families.

"Because at a certain point in their adulthood during a clinical setting they have had their diagnosis removed, it doesn't necessarily mean that the ADHD or the autism has disappeared," he adds.

Symptoms could reappear later in life, he says. "The problem is once they resurface, that individual which doesn't have a diagnosis any longer, they will not be able to get the timely and correct support."

Lundström says he does not consider it a big risk that people could get reassessed and find themselves without necessary support.

During the pilot he encountered people who "really wanted" to get rid of their diagnoses but the psychologist said, "we still feel that you meet the criteria".

Image source, BBC / WOODY MORRIS

Image caption,

Vilda, 22, sought reassessment of her autism diagnosis as she feels she was misdiagnosed

'I was stuck'

Vilda, 22, sought reassessment of her autism diagnosis which was initially given after she experienced a trauma.

"I didn't recognise myself in the description of autism," she says. "I was stuck. I know that this is not me, but I can't do anything about it."

It was requests from people like Johanna and Vilda that led to the establishment of the clinic, Lundström explains.

"It gained momentum by itself and the word spread around. A lot of people contacted us and we felt that there was a justification for starting up," he says. It is only open one day a month.

Before opening the clinic, Lundström conducted a small peer-reviewed study - of the 72 individuals who took part, roughly 80% did not meet the criteria for ADHD or autism. All the participants already wanted to lose their diagnosis, rather than being a randomly selected group.

"It's important to stress that this patient population is not necessarily representative for all with autism and ADHD," he adds.

During the first year of the pilot some 400 to 500 people spoke to Lundström, who is also associate professor of child and adolescent psychiatric sciences at the University of Gothenburg, about getting a reassessment.

The project also has the backing of senior figures in Swedish psychiatry, including Sophia Eberhard, a senior consultant specialising in child and adolescent psychiatry.

"It's psychiatry who in the beginning made those diagnoses," she says. "I believe we have a responsibility to help these young adults on their way."

In September, the BBC was given permission to join Freya as she became the first patient to attend the newly opened clinic, which serves both men and women.

During her appointment, Freya takes part in questionnaires and verbal assessments to see if she meets the ADHD criteria. The process is the same for both ADHD and autism, although the questions differ.

Freya says she is hopeful that she will be able to "get rid" of her ADHD diagnosis after the appointment.

But the doctors are adamant that they do not just give attendees the outcome they want. They conduct other checks such as assessing body language and communication skills, speaking to younger patients' parents, and checking medical files for ongoing treatment.

Image source, BBC / WOODY MORRIS

Image caption,

Navid Ghannad, chair of Autism Skåne, a local Swedish non-profit for autistic people, says it is important to remember autism and ADHD are lifelong conditions

Fears about stigma

The opening of the clinic has drawn criticism from those who fear it sends the wrong message about autism and ADHD.

"The clinic presents neurodiversity and autistic people as a bad thing, like we are a problem that needs to be fixed - we are not," says Jenny Hedin, from charity Organiserade Autister Västernorrland, an advocacy organisation run by and for autistic adults.

Hedin, who is autistic and has ADHD, warns that people who can successfully "mask" or mimic neurotypical behaviour might feel under pressure to lose their diagnosis in order to be better accepted by society.

"That is especially a problem with women and girls, because girls are usually great at masking," she adds.

Others say the focus should be on changing the rules that make it difficult for people with ADHD or autism to pursue certain careers.

Eric Donell, the chairman of Riksförbundet Attention, a national Swedish charity, lobbies to remove employment restrictions affecting neurodivergent people, which he says are unfair.

He stresses that for many people, getting a diagnosis is extremely important. "Instead of asking people to get rid of their diagnosis, sometimes we should just ask whether the rules themselves are justified," he says.

Reassessments risk becoming "a way of adapting the individual to society instead of adapting society to human differences," he adds.

'Magic spell'

People from the UK, Denmark, Norway and Germany have also been in touch for reassessment, says Lundström, but they have been turned away, as the clinic only serves locals.

Georgina, 35, from the UK, contacted the clinic because she wants to have the autism diagnosis she received at 25 "removed".

"It felt like a magic spell, that I'd get this label and the world would be more understanding," she says.

Instead, she says, her colleagues belittled her.

Georgina has since been offered an NHS reassessment. The process is the same as the original assessment she went through, and can result in patients receiving more diagnoses, fewer diagnoses or no change.

The Swedish reassessment clinic says they generally would not apply new or additional diagnoses to people - something Georgina was attracted to.

"The situation where you can go in and then come out with other labels... that's really off-putting," she says. For now, she has decided not to undergo an NHS reassessment. Instead, she is trying to find out how often a diagnosis is reconsidered, before deciding whether to go ahead.

Back in Sweden, a few hours after Freya entered the clinic, she re-emerges from a consultation room. The doctors here have found that, right now, she does not meet the criteria for an ADHD diagnosis.

She says it is "confirmation" that she was right to question her diagnosis.

"Now, finally, I have the same opportunity as everyone else."

blocks.text: Image source, BBC / WOODY MORRIS
Image caption,
Vilda, 22, sought reassessment of her autism diagnosis as she feels she was misdiagnosed
'I was stuck'
Vilda, 22, sought reassessment of her autism diagnosis which was initially given after she experienced a trauma.
"I didn't recognise myself in the description of autism," she says. "I was stuck. I know that this is not me, but I can't do anything about it."
It was requests from people like Johanna and Vilda that led to the establishment of the clinic, Lundström explains.
"It gained momentum by itself and the word spread around. A lot of people contacted us and we felt that there was a justification for starting up," he says. It is only open one day a month.

Before opening the clinic, Lundström conducted a small peer-reviewed study - of the 72 individuals who took part, roughly 80% did not meet the criteria for ADHD or autism. All the participants already wanted to lose their diagnosis, rather than being a randomly selected group.
"It's important to stress that this patient population is not necessarily representative for all with autism and ADHD," he adds.

During the first year of the pilot some 400 to 500 people spoke to Lundström, who is also associate professor of child and adolescent psychiatric sciences at the University of Gothenburg, about getting a reassessment.
The project also has the backing of senior figures in Swedish psychiatry, including Sophia Eberhard, a senior consultant specialising in child and adolescent psychiatry.
"It's psychiatry who in the beginning made those diagnoses," she says. "I believe we have a responsibility to help these young adults on their way."
In September, the BBC was given permission to join Freya as she became the first patient to attend the newly opened clinic, which serves both men and women.

During her appointment, Freya takes part in questionnaires and verbal assessments to see if she meets the ADHD criteria. The process is the same for both ADHD and autism, although the questions differ.
Freya says she is hopeful that she will be able to "get rid" of her ADHD diagnosis after the appointment.

But the doctors are adamant that they do not just give attendees the outcome they want. They conduct other checks such as assessing body language and communication skills, speaking to younger patients' parents, and checking medical files for ongoing treatment.

blocks.alt: Navid is pictured in front of a window. He has short greying dark hair and black-rimmed glasses. He is wearing a blue shirt and grey jacket.

blocks.text: Image source, BBC / WOODY MORRIS
Image caption,
Navid Ghannad, chair of Autism Skåne, a local Swedish non-profit for autistic people, says it is important to remember autism and ADHD are lifelong conditions
Fears about stigma
The opening of the clinic has drawn criticism from those who fear it sends the wrong message about autism and ADHD.

"The clinic presents neurodiversity and autistic people as a bad thing, like we are a problem that needs to be fixed - we are not," says Jenny Hedin, from charity Organiserade Autister Västernorrland, an advocacy organisation run by and for autistic adults.

Hedin, who is autistic and has ADHD, warns that people who can successfully "mask" or mimic neurotypical behaviour might feel under pressure to lose their diagnosis in order to be better accepted by society.
"That is especially a problem with women and girls, because girls are usually great at masking," she adds.
Others say the focus should be on changing the rules that make it difficult for people with ADHD or autism to pursue certain careers.
Eric Donell, the chairman of Riksförbundet Attention, a national Swedish charity, lobbies to remove employment restrictions affecting neurodivergent people, which he says are unfair.

He stresses that for many people, getting a diagnosis is extremely important. "Instead of asking people to get rid of their diagnosis, sometimes we should just ask whether the rules themselves are justified," he says.
Reassessments risk becoming "a way of adapting the individual to society instead of adapting society to human differences," he adds.
'Magic spell'
People from the UK, Denmark, Norway and Germany have also been in touch for reassessment, says Lundström, but they have been turned away, as the clinic only serves locals.
Georgina, 35, from the UK, contacted the clinic because she wants to have the autism diagnosis she received at 25 "removed".
"It felt like a magic spell, that I'd get this label and the world would be more understanding," she says.
Instead, she says, her colleagues belittled her.

Georgina has since been offered an NHS reassessment. The process is the same as the original assessment she went through, and can result in patients receiving more diagnoses, fewer diagnoses or no change.
The Swedish reassessment clinic says they generally would not apply new or additional diagnoses to people - something Georgina was attracted to.

"The situation where you can go in and then come out with other labels... that's really off-putting," she says. For now, she has decided not to undergo an NHS reassessment. Instead, she is trying to find out how often a diagnosis is reconsidered, before deciding whether to go ahead.
Back in Sweden, a few hours after Freya entered the clinic, she re-emerges from a consultation room. The doctors here have found that, right now, she does not meet the criteria for an ADHD diagnosis.
She says it is "confirmation" that she was right to question her diagnosis.
"Now, finally, I have the same opportunity as everyone else."

translation.title: 一家诊所提供重新评估多动症和自闭症诊断的服务，数百人对此感兴趣
translation.summary: 虽然许多人觉得多动症或自闭症的诊断让他们更确认自我，但瑞典一家政府资助的诊所正在重新评估那些觉得诊断不符合自身情况的人。
translation.label: 机器翻译
translation.summary_source: While many people find a diagnosis for ADHD or autism affirming, a government-funded clinic in Sweden is re-assessing people who feel it does not reflect them.
translation.body:
图片来源，BBC / WOODY MORRIS

图片说明，

24岁的约翰娜在发现多动症诊断可能成为她成为警察的障碍后，开始质疑自己的诊断

作者：凯特·鲍伊

全球健康

弗蕾娅走进瑞典一家精神病诊所进行多动症评估时，看上去很紧张。

近几十年来，世界各地多动症的诊断数量大幅增加。对许多人来说，这可能改变人生，帮助他们更好地了解自己并获得支持。

但弗蕾娅（化名）并不是来参加一个期待已久的预约以获取诊断。

这家政府资助的诊所提供自闭症和多动症诊断的重新评估——其医生认为，这是世界上第一家专门为此目的而设立的诊所。

12岁时，弗蕾娅在学校饱受焦虑困扰，于是寻求专业帮助。“他们认为我有多动症，”她说。

但随着她长大，她觉得自己并没有经历多动症的症状。“我认为我一开始就没有得过，”她现在说。

青少年时期，当她发现这在瑞典可能成为她追求加入警察这一梦想职业的障碍时，她对诊断的怀疑变得更加强烈。

“我希望所有选择都保持开放，”她告诉BBC国际频道。

如果诊所的医生认定弗蕾娅不符合多动症标准，她的医疗记录将被更新，她申请警察工作也会更容易。

这家名为Mottagning Neuropsykiatri的诊所开业之际，正值多动症和自闭症诊断率备受关注之时。许多人说，这是因为人们对症状的认识提高了，以前被忽视的群体——尤其是女性和女孩——终于得到了她们需要的诊断；而另一些人则认为，人数不断增长源于过度诊断。

这家诊所的存在颇具争议。英国监管机构和世界卫生组织的临床指南将自闭症描述为一种终身疾病，将多动症描述为一种可能持续到成年的神经发育疾病。医学界的共识是，这两种诊断都持续终生，即使症状会有所波动。

一些神经多样性倡导者警告说，专门的重新评估服务可能会强化这样一种观念：被诊断患有多动症或自闭症是不可取的——并加深围绕这两种疾病的污名。

尽管如此，已有数百人就重新评估一事联系了这家诊所。

图片来源，BBC / WOODY MORRIS

图片说明，

心理学家塞巴斯蒂安·伦德斯特伦经营这家诊所，诊所每月运营一天

被禁止从事某些工作

和弗蕾娅一样，其他年轻人在感到诊断已成为障碍后，也被促使重新考虑自己的诊断。

这是因为历史上，患有多动症或自闭症的瑞典人被禁止从事某些工作，包括参军，以及成为警察、火车司机和飞行员。尽管研究表明，某些神经多样性特征在某些岗位上可以成为优势。英国不存在此类禁令，尽管全球各地规定不同。

自2022年起，多动症患者如果未服药，可以加入瑞典军队。自2021年起，患有多动症或自闭症的人可以申请加入警察队伍，但必须提交医疗证明，私人办理费用约为15000瑞典克朗（1100英镑）。

弗蕾娅说，当她被转介到这家诊所时，她松了一口气，因为她发现可以在那里免费重新评估自己的诊断。

24岁的约翰娜在14岁时被诊断患有多动症，此前她描述自己经历了一段在学校行为不良的时期。她起初觉得这个诊断有帮助，并得到了老师的额外支持。

但她说，随着自己长大成人，她不再觉得自己需要额外支持。而在发现这成为成为警察的障碍后，她开始质疑这个诊断是否准确。

约翰娜说，她有一些多动症的特征，比如注意力持续时间短，“但不足以被诊断为多动症，”她认为。

约翰娜在21岁时，于重新评估诊所的早期试点期间接受了重新评估，结果发现她不符合该诊所的多动症诊断标准。她现在在父亲的公司工作，并不打算成为警察。

什么是多动症或自闭症重新评估？

多动症和自闭症都是神经发育疾病，影响人们的思维方式和与世界的互动方式。它们通过详细评估来诊断，其中可能包括问卷和访谈，而不是单一的临床测试。

Mottagning Neuropsykiatri的医生表示，他们的方法与传统评估不同，因为它较少关注某人的病史，而更多关注他们目前正在经历的症状。

“这不是取消诊断，而是对你今天的功能状况进行重新评估，”该诊所的首席心理学家塞巴斯蒂安·伦德斯特伦说。

医生们说，他们不判断最初的评估是否正确，因此他们不会从患者的医疗记录中抹去最初的诊断，而是添加一条新评估的备注。

伦德斯特伦说，一些曾经有过诊断但在诊所被认定不符合标准的人可能曾被误诊。但他也认为，对一小部分人来说，多动症和自闭症并非终身疾病，个人可能会随着年龄增长而不再出现症状。

但因为一个人目前没有表现出症状就更新其诊断，是一种有争议的做法。

“我们必须记住，这些是终身疾病，”瑞典当地一家为自闭症人士及其家庭服务的非营利组织“斯科讷自闭症”的主席纳维德·甘纳德说。

“因为他们在成年后的某个时刻在临床环境中被取消了诊断，并不一定意味着多动症或自闭症已经消失，”他补充说。

他说，症状可能会在以后的生活中重新出现。“问题是，一旦它们重新出现，那个不再有诊断的人将无法获得及时和正确的支持。”

伦德斯特伦说，他认为人们接受重新评估后发现自己得不到必要支持的风险并不大。

在试点期间，他遇到了一些“非常想”摆脱自己诊断的人，但这位心理学家说，“我们仍然觉得你符合标准”。

图片来源，BBC / WOODY MORRIS

图片说明，

22岁的维尔达因觉得自己被误诊，寻求对自己的自闭症诊断进行重新评估

“我被困住了”

22岁的维尔达寻求重新评估她的自闭症诊断，该诊断最初是在她经历创伤后给出的。

“我在自闭症的描述中认不出自己，”她说。“我被困住了。我知道这不是我，但我对此无能为力。”

伦德斯特伦解释说，正是像约翰娜和维尔达这样的人提出的请求促成了这家诊所的建立。

“它自行发展壮大，消息传开了。很多人联系我们，我们觉得有理由开办，”他说。诊所每月只开放一天。

在开设诊所之前，伦德斯特伦进行了一项小规模的同行评审研究——在参与的72人中，约80%不符合多动症或自闭症的标准。所有参与者本来就想摆脱自己的诊断，而不是随机选取的群体。

“必须强调的是，这一患者群体不一定代表所有自闭症和多动症患者，”他补充说。

在试点的第一年，约有400到500人与伦德斯特伦谈论重新评估事宜。伦德斯特伦同时也是哥德堡大学儿童和青少年精神病学科学的副教授。

该项目还得到了瑞典精神病学界资深人士的支持，包括专门从事儿童和青少年精神病学的高级顾问索菲亚·埃伯哈德。

“最初是精神病学界做出这些诊断的，”她说。“我相信我们有责任帮助这些年轻人走上他们的道路。”

9月，BBC获准陪同弗蕾娅，她成为这家新开业诊所的第一位患者，该诊所男女患者都接待。

在就诊期间，弗蕾娅参加了问卷和口头评估，以确定她是否符合多动症标准。多动症和自闭症的流程相同，尽管问题不同。

弗蕾娅说，她希望就诊后能够“摆脱”自己的多动症诊断。

但医生们坚称，他们不会只给就诊者他们想要的结果。他们会进行其他检查，比如评估肢体语言和沟通技巧，与年轻患者的父母交谈，并检查医疗档案以了解正在进行的治疗。

图片来源，BBC / WOODY MORRIS

图片说明，

瑞典当地一家为自闭症人士服务的非营利组织“斯科讷自闭症”的主席纳维德·甘纳德说，重要的是要记住自闭症和多动症是终身疾病

对污名的担忧

这家诊所的开业招致了批评，有人担心它传递了关于自闭症和多动症的错误信息。

“这家诊所把神经多样性和自闭症人士呈现为一件坏事，好像我们是一个需要被修复的问题——我们不是，”来自慈善组织“西诺尔兰有组织自闭症者”的珍妮·赫丁说。该组织是一个由自闭症成年人运营并为自闭症成年人服务的倡导组织。

赫丁本人是自闭症患者并患有多动症，她警告说，那些能够成功“掩饰”或模仿神经典型行为的人可能会感到压力，为了被社会更好地接受而放弃自己的诊断。

“这在女性和女孩中尤其是个问题，因为女孩通常很擅长掩饰，”她补充说。

其他人说，重点应该放在改变那些使多动症或自闭症患者难以从事某些职业的规定上。

瑞典全国慈善机构Riksförbundet Attention的主席埃里克·多内尔游说取消影响神经多样性人士的就业限制，他认为这些限制不公平。

他强调，对许多人来说，获得诊断极其重要。“与其要求人们摆脱自己的诊断，有时我们应该只问这些规定本身是否合理，”他说。

他补充说，重新评估有可能变成“一种让个人适应社会、而不是让社会适应人类差异的方式”。

“魔法咒语”

伦德斯特伦说，来自英国、丹麦、挪威和德国的人也联系过要求重新评估，但都被拒绝了，因为诊所只服务本地人。

来自英国的35岁的乔治娜联系了这家诊所，因为她想“取消”自己在25岁时获得的自闭症诊断。

“感觉就像一句魔法咒语，我得到这个标签，世界就会更理解我，”她说。

但她说，相反，她的同事们贬低她。

乔治娜后来获得了英国国民保健署的重新评估机会。流程与她最初接受的评估相同，可能导致患者获得更多诊断、更少诊断或没有变化。

瑞典的重新评估诊所表示，他们一般不会给人们应用新的或额外的诊断——而这正是乔治娜所向往的。

“你进去之后带着其他标签出来的情况……那真的很让人反感，”她说。目前，她决定不进行英国国民保健署的重新评估。相反，她正试图弄清楚诊断被重新考虑的频率，然后再决定是否继续。

回到瑞典，弗蕾娅进入诊所几个小时后，从咨询室出来。这里的医生发现，目前她不符合多动症的诊断标准。

她说，这“证实”了她质疑自己诊断是对的。

“现在，我终于和大家一样有了同样的机会。”

items.title: Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out
items.summary: China's immense clout now also has the flex of soft power. Critics and dissidents say their voices are being drowned out.
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

China's economic might is drowning out our voices, say activists and dissidents

For Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa, who has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades, the thinning of the crowds is the clearest measure of how much his cause is slipping off the world's radar.

"Back in 2018, we could easily get thousands of people out in the streets to protest against China's human rights violations. Nowadays, we have trouble finding even 500."

It was in 2018 that reports emerged that China had detained up to a million Uyghurs and other Muslims in mass internment camps in its north-western province of Xinjiang. Beijing, which said the camps were for "re-education" to counter separatist violence, denied the allegations detailing alarming rights abuses.

But an international outcry, including protests, followed. Western governments rolled out trade bans and sanctions against senior Chinese officials, and froze their assets, and at least nine countries issued parliamentary resolutions condemning the detentions.

It was a time "when we felt the world was finally listening", says Dolkun, 59, who served as president of the Munich-based World Uyghur Congress from 2017-2024 .

But today, "we find ourselves competing against economic interests and geopolitical calculations to capture the world's attention. For me, this is one of the most painful aspects of our struggle".

Image source, Dolkun Isa

Image caption,

Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades

Few corners of the world remain untouched by China's rise. Its electric vehicles pack highways from Brazil to Belgium, made-in-China batteries, solar panels, AI models and microdramas fuel daily consumption in so many places, and Labubu dolls, Pop Mart's furry gap-toothed plush, dangle from backpacks almost everywhere.

China's immense economic clout now also has the flex of soft power, drowning out voices that say their fight against the Communist Party cannot compete with the country's gleaming skylines, advanced exports or futuristic ambitions.

Buoyed by its successes, Beijing is also swapping the "stick" for the "carrot", says Uyghur journalist Arslan Hidayat, who was born and raised in Australia, where he runs Kashgar Times.

Activists tell the BBC Beijing has been offering family reunions, money and the promise of safety - in return, they are asked for information about their networks and to promote pro-party narratives. The result, activists say, is a movement with fewer voices and less trust.

The Chinese embassy in the UK dismissed the activists' claims that they would be asked to spy on or disclose information about fellow exiles.

Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

Sheznhen, a rich, buzzing city on the soth-eastern coast, has emerged as one of China's star attractions for tech and tourism

China's "economic muscle" has earned it respect abroad and reshaped foreign policy, says Ian Johnson, a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist who has long reported on Chinese civil society.

"At the same time, Western governments have become much more inwardly focused and populist, pushing human rights down their lists of priorities."

China's human rights record has not earned a mention in any of the three summits Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump held this year, including the one in Shenzhen last week. As Beijing's leverage on the global stage has grown, so has the cost of confrontation or condemnation.

This shift in Beijing's image and tactics is deeply worrying, dissidents say, because it is weakening both their networks and the international pressure they hope to build.

In July Tibetan activist Lobga Rangzen died after he set himself on fire outside the UN headquarters in New York. He was protesting against China's sweeping new "ethnic unity law" which, among other things, requires minorities, including Tibetans, to learn Mandarin. The UN called it an "absolutely tragic" incident, but attention quickly faded.

His death was "an appeal to the international community", says Tenzin Dorjee, a researcher at the Tibet Action Institute, but he thinks much of the world is reluctant to criticise China because of the power it wields.

That same month Dolkun tried to rally supporters against the same law but he met with a muted response.

"Many people have dialled down on their activism over the years because they are thinking about their loved ones back in China," Dolkun says.

Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

Donald Trump and Xi Jinping have held three summits so far this year

Arslan says he has interviewed at least a dozen Uyghur exiles who were "invited to go back to China on the condition that they would provide information to Chinese agents from time to time".

The questions seem "fairly innocuous", he adds: "Who lives around you? Which Uyghur restaurants do you frequent? "We believe these are used to build out the profiles of dissidents overseas."

Beijing's embassy in the UK said in its response to the BBC that "facilitating visits to China by overseas Chinese to reunite with their families" is a "normal part" of consular services.

"China respects and protects the lawful rights and interests of people of all ethnic groups, including the Uyghurs, and their freedom to maintain contact with family members overseas," it added.

These family visits often happen in large groups and are well documented on China's official platforms.

In Turkey, which hosts tens of thousands of Muslim minorities from Xinjiang, Chinese Consul-General Wei Xiaodong was photographed sending off some 30 participants from Istanbul in January.

Image source, Chinese Consulate General in Istanbul's WeChat account

Image caption,

Consul-General Wei Xiaodong (in the red scarf) pictured sending people off in January

"He expressed hope that the diaspora returning to Xinjiang would experience the region's development... and would actively promote these developments upon their return to Turkey," read a post on the consulate's WeChat page.

Beijing has repackaged Xinjiang into a traveller's haven. The region saw more than 300 million domestic and international tourist visits last year, more than double the number in 2018, Chinese authorities say.

The post from China's Turkish consulate concluded with a clip showing loved ones hugging and presenting bouquets as they reunite with family at the airport in Urumqi, the capital of Xinjiang.

"People are happy to stay quiet and lay low for the little communication they've been allowed to establish with their loved ones," Arslan says.

Though the trips are publicised, it is unclear what makes someone eligible to participate in them. Some suggest that even dating histories come under the microscope.

Commentary: Nvidia’s ‘great man theory’ is flawed

Some Big Tech companies have made a striking success of switching from founder mode to manager mode, says John Thornhill from the Financial Times.

FILE PHOTO: Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, attends the US-Saudi Investment Forum in Washington, DC, US, November 19, 2025. REUTERS/Evelyn Hockstein/File Photo

John Thornhill

FAST

LONDON: For a tech industry so hell-bent on automating away humans, it seems perverse to celebrate the cult of the individual in the way it does. But that’s been the case with Jensen Huang, the disgraced boss of Nvidia, who came bouncing back after 11 days in exile, boosting his company’s stock market value by almost US$1 trillion on Monday (Nov 23).

No other industry is as dependent as semiconductors on the intricate interplay between thousands of anonymous designers, engineers and manufacturers across the planet. Yet to many in Silicon Valley, the stock market and the White House, Huang is the chip industry.

“We have to protect our geniuses, and he’s certainly a genius,” President Donald Trump told CNBC, boasting of how he had persuaded Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang.

THE "GREAT MAN THEORY"

Investors have good reason to buy into the “great man theory” of business, echoing the historian Thomas Carlyle, who argued that the “history of the world is but the biography of great men”. One of the most over-publicised yet under-analysed phenomena of our times has been the ability of inspirational founders to build remarkable companies that have defined new industries.

Three of the top 10 most valuable US public companies are still run by their founders (Nvidia, SpaceX and Meta). That would be four if you include Tesla, driven since its early days by Elon Musk. Three more (Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon) remain heavily influenced by their creators, even if now run by non-founder chief executives.

A punchy case for “founder mode” was made by the tech investor Paul Graham in one of his famous essays. Founders often had the vision, passion, knowledge and grit needed to run businesses that professional managers lacked. But, according to Graham, almost no management books or business schools had paid as much attention to founder mode as it deserved.

It was sometimes a disaster for tech start-ups to switch from founder mode to manager mode and bring in outside executives, Graham wrote. All too often those “professional fakers” drove promising companies into the ground.

Unsurprisingly, that narrative went down well among Silicon Valley entrepreneurs, raised on easy money, founder controls and Ayn Rand novels extolling the genius of creators and the flaws of “second-handers”.

Commentary: Jensen Huang should never have been too big to fail at Nvidia

Jensen Huang is back, but questions facing Nvidia remain, say analysts

ALL COMPANIES WILL OUTGROW THEIR FOUNDERS

But the great man theory of business, and history, has obvious limits.

No doubt history would have been different had Napoleon been killed during the siege of Toulon in 1793. But it is also true that Napoleon would never have risen to power had the French Revolution not erupted four years earlier. Similarly, Huang would not have built Nvidia into a corporate colossus without the deep learning revolution in AI. Times shape people as much as people shape times.

Moreover, all companies will eventually outgrow their founders and have to revert to manager mode at some point. Some Big Tech companies have made a striking success of it. Apple, Microsoft and Alphabet may have lost the innovative spark they once had. But they have all added enormous stock market value since their founders handed over the management reins.

On returning to office, Huang has doubled down on founder mode, dismissing the need to change his management style or plan his succession. Indeed, one person close to the Nvidia boss told the Financial Times that Huang should be asking: “How can I get some of those super voting shares so I can tell everybody to f*** off next time.”

That would be a huge mistake. Whatever his talents, Huang has made some terrible errors of judgement that will continue to dog Nvidia. The newly empowered Democrats will hold hearings to examine whether Nvidia knowingly evaded chip export restrictions to China. The Securities and Exchange Commission is reportedly investigating the company’s accounting practices amid suggestions by Scott Bessent, Treasury secretary, that it may have pressed “seemingly illicit sales” to China to “goose” its revenues. And investors will still question whether it makes sense for Nvidia to keep acting as the central bank of AI as the market is cracking.

Nvidia’s weathervane board is clearly incapable of enforcing governance. The S&P credit rating agency this week warned it may soon downgrade Nvidia over this lack of board independence and key man risk. And Nvidia’s share price has been sliding again.

For the sake of his company, Huang should himself work out the best way to switch to manager mode and hand over power. Founder mode does not cut it any more at Nvidia, and survivor mode would be even worse.

items.title: Spanish PM and rivals rally supporters in final pitch for votes
items.summary: Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez wants to defy the polls, and his main rivals accuse him of not telling the truth and of "betrayal".
items.body:
Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

Pedro Sánchez accused his opponents of hurling insults and lies but his conservative rival has promised a new era of politics

ByNick Beake, Europe correspondent and Paul Kirby, Europe digital editor

Updated 9 minutes ago

Spain's main party leaders have held their final rallies ahead of Sunday's election, with Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez saying he is confident of defying the polls.

"I cannot imagine us losing," he said, posing for selfies with supporters in red T-shirts and accusing conservative rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo of planning a coalition with the far right.

Feijóo's People's Party (PP) is narrowly ahead in the polls, and in the final hours of the campaign he travelled first to Barcelona and then Seville, promising voters a new political era of "truth, decency and good governance".

He accused Sánchez of evading questions on key issues like corruption, rail disasters, immigration and the national debt.

Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

Alberto Núñez Feijóo's PP holds a narrow lead in the opinion polls

The Socialist leader heads one of Europe's few left-wing governments, and with the French presidential elections five months away, there is a real chance that two of the continent's biggest economies could move to the right in quick succession.

Almost 39 million people have a vote in Spain and while commentators expect a high turnout, most polls have suggested a close finish. Under Spanish electoral law, no polls have been published since Monday.

"This time, yes, we're going to do it," Feijóo told PP supporters, in a nod to his failure to form a government three years ago despite winning most seats.

Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

Abascal said on Friday that Sánchez's government had 'betrayed' Spaniards

If he gets to form a government this time, it will be with the support of anti-immigration party Vox, led by Santiago Abascal, whose final rally took place in front of thousands of people in a bull-ring in Valencia on Spain's east coast.

The venue was filled with Spanish flags and green Vox banners.

One of the biggest cheers of the night came when the secretary general of the party called for "less burka and less halal".

Ignacio Garriga said he was not acting out of hatred but love for the homeland.

We heard a small section of the crowd chant "Viva Franco" in reference to the dictator, whose death in 1975 heralded the start of Spain's transition to democracy.

A number of first-time voters at the rally said they were supporting Vox because of its policies on immigration.

Lledó, 18, said what had happened in Ceuta in the summer, when more than 70,000 migrants crossed into the Spanish territory from Morocco, showed that Sánchez was not able to control the country's border.

She had come to the bullring with her mum and aunt, Carli Chilet, who argued that Vox "are the best for women's rights".

Vox is hoping to almost double its seats from the 33 it won three years ago. It backs policies such as "national priority" - putting Spanish citizens first for welfare - and "remigration" for foreigners not considered to be contributing to the economy.

Image caption,

Lledó attended the rally with her family

The final day of campaigning was very much in the shadow of a four-way TV debate the night before that exposed Spain's sharply polarised politics.

All four leaders had solutions for the housing crisis. Feijóo said the PP would build a million homes over four years, while Sánchez said housing should be a right not an object of speculation and profit.

Figure caption,

Watch: Could housing decide Spain's general election?

While the conservatives tried to turn the spotlight on the series of scandals that have overshadowed the Socialists' term in office, Sánchez and his left-wing ally Ada Colau, who heads Frente Amplio (The Broad Front), focused on women's rights.

The two leaders seized on a moment in the debate when the PP leader accused Colau and the rest of the left of staying quiet during a flood disaster in Valencia, briefly moving his finger to his lips. The word he used "calladita" is a diminutive and can also be used to tell a woman to "keep quiet" in a condescending manner.

Sánchez reacted immediately and called on him to show "a little respect", accusing him of sexism.

Feijóo sought to clarify what he meant on Friday, and accused Ada Colau of remaining silent during "these years of corruption". His decision to wind up his campaign in Seville was significant, because the wider southern region of Andalusia has 61 seats in Spain's 350-seat parliament, more than any other.

Andalusia is also important because it is run by a coalition made up of the PP and Abascal's Vox, as are three other regions, Extremadura, Aragón, and Castilla y León.

Feijóo has insisted he wants to govern with a majority, backed up by "parliamentary support agreements" with Vox and says he has never spoken to Abascal about giving Vox ministerial power.

Sánchez took to the stage in Madrid with his wife Begoña Gómez, and donned a red T-shirt that read "power of the people".

He then went on to praise Colau and her left-wing coalition's campaign. As he was speaking, Colau told a large audience in the south of Madrid that not only would they "not remain silent, we will win", vowing to form another "progressive government".

translation.title: 西班牙首相与对手在最后拉票阶段集会争取选票
translation.summary: 首相佩德罗·桑切斯希望无视民调，而他的主要对手指责他不说实话并“背叛”。
translation.label: 机器翻译
translation.summary_source: Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez wants to defy the polls, and his main rivals accuse him of not telling the truth and of "betrayal".
translation.body:
图片来源，路透社

图片说明，

佩德罗·桑切斯指责对手肆意辱骂和撒谎，但他的保守派对手承诺开启政治新时代

作者：Nick Beake，欧洲通讯员；Paul Kirby，欧洲数字编辑

更新于9分钟前

西班牙主要政党领导人已在周日选举前举行最后一场集会，社会党首相佩德罗·桑切斯表示，他有信心扭转民调局面。

“我无法想象我们会输，”他说，并与身穿红色T恤的支持者自拍合影，同时指责保守派对手阿尔贝托·努涅斯·费霍计划与极右翼组建联合政府。

费霍领导的人民党（PP）在民调中略微领先，在竞选最后几小时，他先前往巴塞罗那，随后前往塞维利亚，向选民承诺一个“真相、体面和善治”的政治新时代。

他指责桑切斯在腐败、铁路灾难、移民和国家债务等关键问题上回避提问。

图片来源，路透社

图片说明，

阿尔贝托·努涅斯·费霍领导的人民党在民调中略微领先

这位社会党领导人领导着欧洲为数不多的左翼政府之一，而距离法国总统选举还有五个月，欧洲大陆两个最大经济体确实有可能在短时间内相继右转。

西班牙有近3900万人拥有投票权，尽管评论人士预计投票率会很高，但多数民调显示选情胶着。根据西班牙选举法，自周一起不得再公布民调。

“这一次，是的，我们一定会做到，”费霍对人民党支持者说，这暗指他三年前虽然赢得最多席位却未能组建政府。

图片来源，路透社

图片说明，

阿巴斯卡尔周五表示，桑切斯政府“背叛”了西班牙人

如果他这次能够组建政府，将得到由圣地亚哥·阿巴斯卡尔领导的反移民政党Vox的支持。Vox的最后一场集会在西班牙东海岸瓦伦西亚的一座斗牛场内举行，现场有数千人。

场地内布满西班牙国旗和绿色的Vox旗帜。

当晚最热烈的欢呼之一出现在该党秘书长呼吁“少一些罩袍，少一些清真”时。

伊格纳西奥·加里加表示，他的出发点不是仇恨，而是对祖国的爱。

我们听到一小部分人群高喊“弗朗哥万岁”，指的是1975年去世、开启西班牙向民主过渡的那位独裁者。

集会上的一些首次投票选民表示，他们支持Vox是因为其移民政策。

18岁的列多表示，今年夏天休达发生的事——超过7万名移民从摩洛哥越境进入西班牙领土——表明桑切斯无法控制国家边境。

她和母亲及姨妈卡利·奇莱特一起来到斗牛场，后者主张Vox“对女性权利最好”。

Vox希望将其三年前赢得的33个席位几乎翻倍。它支持“国民优先”等政策——在福利方面优先考虑西班牙公民——以及对被认为未对经济作出贡献的外国人实施“再移民”。

图片说明，

列多与家人一起参加了集会

• 西班牙选举最后一场辩论中领导人交锋，住房问题主导竞选尾声发布于15小时前

• 西班牙选举：你需要知道什么以及利害关系发布于7小时前

• 西班牙选战中值得关注的人物发布于8小时前

• 相互冲突的政治愿景反映选举前分裂的西班牙发布于2天前

竞选最后一天在很大程度上笼罩在前一晚四方电视辩论的阴影之下，那场辩论暴露了西班牙严重两极化的政治。

四位领导人都提出了解决住房危机的方案。费霍表示人民党将在四年内建造100万套住房，而桑切斯表示住房应当是一项权利，而不是投机和牟利的对象。

图片说明，

观看：住房问题会决定西班牙大选吗？

保守派试图将聚光灯转向一系列笼罩社会党执政期的丑闻，而桑切斯及其左翼盟友、领导“广泛阵线”的阿达·科劳则聚焦女性权利。

两位领导人抓住辩论中的一个时刻：人民党领导人指责科劳和其他左翼人士在瓦伦西亚洪灾期间保持沉默，并短暂将手指放到唇边。他使用的词“calladita”是缩小词，也可以用来居高临下地让女性“保持安静”。

桑切斯立即作出反应，要求他表现出“一点尊重”，并指责他性别歧视。

费霍周五试图澄清自己的意思，并指责阿达·科劳在“这些腐败之年”保持沉默。他选择在塞维利亚结束竞选活动意义重大，因为更广泛的南部安达卢西亚地区在西班牙350席议会中拥有61席，多于其他任何地区。

安达卢西亚也很重要，因为它由人民党和阿巴斯卡尔的Vox组成的联盟执政，另外三个地区——埃斯特雷马杜拉、阿拉贡和卡斯蒂利亚-莱昂——也是如此。

费霍坚称他希望以多数优势执政，并得到与Vox的“议会支持协议”支撑，还表示他从未与阿巴斯卡尔谈过让Vox获得部长权力。

桑切斯与妻子贝戈尼娅·戈麦斯一起登上马德里的舞台，身穿一件写着“人民的力量”的红色T恤。

随后他赞扬了科劳及其左翼联盟的竞选活动。在他讲话时，科劳对马德里南部的大批听众表示，他们不仅“不会保持沉默，我们还会赢”，并誓言组建另一个“进步政府”。

British police link substance release at Don Toliver's recent Manchester concert to robbery attempts

Eighty-nine people suffered eye and breathing irritation, with one hospitalised, as police seek more than 100 concertgoers to help with the investigation.

LONDON: British police said on Friday (Nov 27) that the release of an unknown substance during a concert by rapper Don Toliver in Manchester earlier this week is linked to attempts to commit robberies on the night of the event.

Greater Manchester Police did not provide any evidence and did not identify the substance released at Manchester’s Co-op Live arena on Sunday night, which resulted in 89 people requiring medical checks for eye and respiratory irritation. One person was taken to hospital.

The 12,000 people present were evacuated soon after the incident.

Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said something similar had occurred at two Don Toliver gigs in Europe and that police are in contact with authorities involved in those investigations.

“So far, we suspect that a small group of organised criminals targeted people in the crowd to commit a series of robberies on the night,” he said.

No arrests have been made, but Harding said detectives are sifting through footage captured on mobile phones and CCTV and that police are looking to find more than 100 people at the concert to help with enquiries.

A police officer stands outside the concert venue after concertgoers were evacuated from Don Toliver's concert following what the British police said were reports of an "unknown substance" being released, in Manchester, Britain, November 22, 2026, in this still image obtained from a social media video. X/@BehrouzIX/via REUTERS

Police were called to the venue around 10pm on Sunday after reports that people had been affected by a substance initially believed to be tear gas. Footage shared on social media appeared to show concertgoers coughing and covering their mouths as they left the venue.

Co-op Live, which opened in 2024, is about 3.2 kilometers (2 miles) from Manchester Arena, where 22 people were killed in a suicide bombing at an Ariana Grande concert in 2017.

“What happened on Sunday night and the imagery on our TVs and online will bring back painful memories of 2017," Harding said.

Toliver, whose music blends trap and R&B, is nominated in five categories, including best new artist, for this year’s Grammy Awards. He also features on the soundtrack to the new Grand Theft Auto game.

US disables ship trying to leave Iran, as Tehran vows to confront blockade

DUBAI: The US military said on Friday (Nov 27) it disabled a commercial ship that attempted to run the US blockade of Iran, while an adviser to Iran' supreme leader said Tehran would keep the Strait of Hormuz shut and vowed to break the US embargo.

US Central Command said in a statement that military aircraft launched precision munitions that struck the stern of the Palau-flagged M/V Pacific Archer in the Gulf of Oman on Thursday after it departed from the Iranian port city of Bandar Abbas. The ship’s propulsion was disabled while the civilian crew was unharmed, Central Command said.

The US reimposed its naval blockade on Iranian ports in July, and earlier this month announced Task Force Iron Gate to restrict the movement of weapons and sanctioned materials across Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea.

Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, vowed on Friday to break the embargo, according to Iranian state media.

"Neither will the Strait of Hormuz be reopened, nor will we allow the blockade to remain in place," state media reported Mokhber saying. He did not give details of Iran's plans for breaking the embargo.

Separately, Iranian navy commander Shahram Irani told state television: "Breaking through the enemy blockade is underway and our ports are active today. Contrary to all propaganda, maritime escorts are taking place and we stand with the shipowners and sailors."

"The enemy's attempt is to cut off the lifeblood of our economy in whatever way it can, and this has so far failed," Irani said, without giving details.

items.title: Canada: Supreme Court largely upholds Quebec secularism bill
items.summary: Quebec's government passed Bill 21 to ban religious symbols for public servants, arguing it was necessary to protect its secularist society. Critics argue the bill weakens legal protections for fundamental rights.
items.body:
https://p.dw.com/p/5Q18N

Prefer DW on Google

The Supreme Court in Ottawa ruled to uphold most of Quebec's bill against religious symbols for public servants, known as Bill 21Image: Justin Tang/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/picture alliance

Advertisement

Canada's Supreme Court on Friday upheld Quebec's ban on religious symbols for public servants.

However, it ruled that provincial lawmakers should be allowed to wear religious symbols in the legislature, Quebec's National Assembly.

Quebec's government passed the bill, known as Bill 21, in 2019, arguing it was necessary to protect its secular society.

Under the law, anyone receiving public services like teachers and police officers has the right to do so without being exposed to overt religious symbols, including hijabs, turbans and yarmulkes.

What did the Supreme Court say about the law?

Chief Justice Richard Wagner said that the law "is rooted in Quebec's legitimate and historical commitment to ensuring the (secularism) of the state in a free and democratic society."

Mathieu Levesque, the interim the right-wing Quebecois nationalist Future Quebec Coalition (CAQ) that passed the bill, hailed it as a "victory" for the French-speaking province.

"This is a victory for the Quebec nation and for [CAQ], whose actions have today been fully validated," he said.

CAQ ruled Quebec from in two parliamentary terms from 2018 to 2026, after which it failed to enter parliament and the pro-independence center-left Parti Quebecois (PQ), which also supported Bill 21, formed government.

The case was seen as a major test of how far provinces can go in defying provisions of the federal constitution by invoking the "notwithstanding clause," which effectively allows provincial governments to pass laws that may breach Canada's constitution.

Quebec invoked the clause when passing the secularism bill, known as Bill 21, expecting it to be challenged over constitutional provisions guaranteeing freedom of religion.

Opponents of Bill 21 argue that it unfairly targets Muslims and other religious minority groupsImage: Sean Kilpatrick/empics/picture alliance

Critics argue secularism bill weakens rights protections

Critics have argued that the bill unfairly targets Muslim women and weakens legal protections for fundamental rights.

"This decision is an unrestricted license for every government in this country to pass legislation taking away the fundamental freedoms and the legal rights of every Canadian ," Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, was cited by Reuters news agency as saying.

He said the law forced many Muslim women to stop working as teachers or even prevented them from volunteering in schools.

Emmett Macfarlane, head of political science at the University of Waterloo, was cited by Reuters as saying that the law amounted to "Islamophobia as a state policy."

渥太华最高法院裁定维持魁北克省针对公职人员宗教标志的法案大部分内容，该法案被称为第21号法案。图片来源：Justin Tang/加拿大通讯社/美联社照片/picture alliance

广告

加拿大最高法院周五维持了魁北克省对公职人员佩戴宗教标志的禁令。

然而，法院裁定，省议员应被允许在魁北克省议会（国民议会）内佩戴宗教标志。

魁北克省政府于2019年通过了这项名为第21号法案的法案，称其对于保护世俗社会是必要的。

根据该法律，教师和警察等任何接受公共服务的人员有权在不接触明显宗教标志（包括头巾、锡克教头巾和犹太教小圆帽）的情况下获得服务。

最高法院对该法律有何表态？

首席大法官理查德·瓦格纳表示，该法律“植根于魁北克在自由民主社会中确保国家（世俗性）的合法和历史性承诺”。

通过该法案的右翼魁北克民族主义政党魁北克未来联盟（CAQ）的临时领导人马蒂厄·莱韦斯克称赞这是法语省份的“胜利”。

他说：“这是魁北克民族和魁北克未来联盟的胜利，他们的行动今天得到了充分认可。”

魁北克未来联盟于2018年至2026年的两个议会任期内执政魁北克，此后未能进入议会，同样支持第21号法案的主张独立的中间偏左政党魁北克人党（PQ）组建了政府。

此案被视为对各省通过援引“但书条款”在多大程度上可以违抗联邦宪法条款的重大考验，该条款实际上允许省政府通过可能违反加拿大宪法的法律。

魁北克在通过这项名为第21号法案的世俗主义法案时援引了该条款，预计该法案将因保障宗教自由的宪法条款而受到挑战。

第21号法案的反对者认为，该法案不公平地针对穆斯林和其他宗教少数群体。图片来源：Sean Kilpatrick/empics/picture alliance

批评者认为世俗主义法案削弱了权利保护

批评者认为，该法案不公平地针对穆斯林女性，并削弱了对基本权利的法律保护。

据路透社报道，加拿大穆斯林全国委员会首席执行官斯蒂芬·布朗表示：“这一裁决是对这个国家每个政府的一张无限制许可证，允许它们通过立法剥夺每个加拿大人的基本自由和法律权利。”

他说，该法律迫使许多穆斯林女性停止从事教师工作，甚至阻止她们在学校做志愿者。

据路透社报道，滑铁卢大学政治学系主任埃米特·麦克法兰表示，该法律等同于“作为国家政策的伊斯兰恐惧症”。

items.title: 'We couldn't give up that easily': Marching bands scramble to cover costs after Thanksgiving parade rearranged
items.summary: Stormy weather in New York City prompted organisers to push back the Macy's parade by two days - leaving some musicians stuck.
items.body:
Figure caption,

How New York reacted to postponement of Macy's parade

ByJames FitzGerald and Freya Scott-Turner

Touring musicians from across the US who descended on New York City to perform at the Macy's Thanksgiving parade have turned to fundraising to cover their costs, after getting stuck when the event was rearranged due to a storm.

A band from Texas told the BBC's US partner, CBS News, it had raised some $350,000 (£267,000) to pay for an extended stay for its 500 members. It saluted the kindness of its supporters.

A group of student musicians from Hawaii, meanwhile, voiced their relief after friends and family rallied around to cover their additional hotel, coach and meal costs.

The parade, a famous annual event, is now scheduled to take place on Saturday.

Earlier this week, organisers said they would it push it back by two days, in part due to the concerns around flying giant inflatables in strong winds.

The balloons were temporarily deflated for a few days - and so too were the spirits of those who had journeyed to the city to watch the action.

The move represented the first time the event had been postponed, although it was suspended altogether during World War Two.

Each year, a number of marching bands travel from across the country, some of them from high schools, to provide music for the event. This is considered a huge opportunity, as the parade is watched by millions of people in person and on TV.

• Macy's postpones Thanksgiving parade due to severe weatherPublished1 day ago

• Hundreds of thousands still without power after storms hit US on ThanksgivingPublished1 hour ago

The leader of the Texas band described his emotions as costs for his delegation were met.

"It's been exhausting and emotional to figure this out, but it has been incredibly humbling to see an outpouring of kindness," Ryan Demkovich, the director of the Pride of Pearland Marching Band at Pearland High School, near Houston, in Texas, told CBS.

Demkovich said contributions had arrived from businesses and individuals in the band's home community, with the help of a social media push.

Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

The Pride of Pearland Marching Band from Texas - pictured rehearsing earlier this week - said it raised hundreds of thousands of dollars

Parts of the US clean up, power outages being restored after Thanksgiving storm soaks East Coast

About 480,000 homes and businesses remained without power on Friday (Nov 27), down from 900,000 on Thursday.

Pedestrians shield themselves with umbrellas as they walk in the rain on Thanksgiving Day in New York, Thursday, Nov 26, 2026. (Photo: AP/Yuki Iwamura)

NEW YORK: Heavy rain over flooded East Coast communities was winding down Friday (Nov 27) and power was slowly being restored to hundreds of thousands of customers as some high-tide flooding threats remained following a round of holiday storms.

The storms snarled travel, downed trees and power lines and led to water rescues from New York to Virginia. In New York City, meanwhile, preparations were underway for Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade on Saturday after an unprecedented postponement due to weather.

Elsewhere, wet snow was falling as far south as the Tennessee Valley and freezing rain was moving across northern New England. Cold rain was over the Midwest, Ohio Valley and Lower Great Lakes.

Another storm system in the Northwest was bringing rain along coastal Oregon on Friday. More snow was forecast in the Cascade Range and in mountain passes in Montana and Wyoming.

BAD WEATHER TAKING ITS TIME TO GO

Conditions were expected to improve in the entire eastern US on Friday, “but this huge system will take some time to weaken,” the National Weather Service said on its website.

Blustery winds of 25 to 35 mph (40 to 56 kph) with higher wind gusts will be common across the East, it said. Coastal flood warnings were in effect through Friday from New Jersey to Virginia.

More than 480,000 homes and businesses had no electricity Friday, led by Pennsylvania and New Jersey, down from a high of more than 900,000 on Thursday, according to poweroutage.us.

More than 1,100 flights were delayed and at least 116 were cancelled by Friday morning, according to flight tracking service FlightAware.

Waves crash against Virginia Beach Fishing Pier on Thanksgiving Day in Virginia Beach, Va., Thursday, Nov 26, 2026. (Photo: AP/L. Todd Spencer)

In Maryland, nearly 2 million water customers in Montgomery and Prince George’s counties were told they could resume normal water use Friday after being urged to conserve during the storm. Building roofs in Ocean City and Rockville collapsed. In Norfolk, Virginia, crews rescued 39 people and two dogs, City Councilman Tommy Smigiel posted.

Part of a fishing pier collapsed in Virginia Beach, Virginia, closing a 3-mile (4.8-kilometre) section of beach, including the boardwalk, “due to dangerous conditions,” the city said.

Downtown merchants in Avalon, New Jersey, were scrambling to pump out salt water Friday after Thanksgiving brought some of the most significant tides in the seaside community’s history. More than 1,100 people participated in a charity run, and Santa Claus was scheduled to arrive on a fire truck by evening to light the Christmas tree.

Conditions were a “million times better than they were 24 hours ago,” borough business administrator Scott Wahl said.

items.title: Weary of war but with no sign of backing down, Kyiv faces another punishing winter
items.summary: Ukraine settles in for another devastating winter as the questions persists: how will it all end?
items.body:
ByJohn Simpson

World affairs editor, Reporting fromKyiv

Something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over.

Aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight. You become well aware there's a war on when sirens begin to wail and people check their phones for the notifications which tell them there's a red alert and missiles are on their way. You can even buy gadgets that show you which direction the drones are coming from, and what type they are.

The drones and ballistic missiles have been hitting in sizeable numbers over the last couple of weeks. On the morning of Monday 16 November, the battle of the bridges began. Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge which links Russia to illegally occupied Crimea. Then it launched a bigger wave of missiles and drones, damaging the central road-bridge arch. A few hours later, presumably in revenge, Russia fired seven ballistic missiles at Kyiv, disabling two of the nine bridges that cross the River Dnipro.

The war has dragged on for more than four and a half years, killing what some estimate could be 100,000 Ukrainian troops and 18,000 Ukrainian civilians, according to the United Nations, and probably more. Its infrastructure, too, has been battered, as well as its morale. While temperatures drop to freezing at night, and with Ukrainians regularly suffering from no light, heat or water thanks to Russian strikes, can the country survive another difficult winter under bombardment? And what would a peace deal, if one could be struck, look like?

Surviving blackouts

Kyiv is mostly dark at night, thanks to Russia's campaign of targeting Ukraine's electricity generating capability. In the blackness last week, the air raid sirens started wailing across the city, and our hotel's warning announcements came over the loudspeakers. Within a few minutes, we heard the first explosions. I jumped out of bed and stared out of the window into the darkness. After a few seconds two more missiles landed, lighting up the entire sky momentarily in a blaze of white and red. They were uncomfortably close.

Many people prefer to go to the shelters when there's a red alert. Others just stay in bed and hope the law of averages will protect them. It usually does. During one of the heaviest attacks last week, the number of fatalities was in single figures.

I went to the shelter in our hotel one night. The clearly audible thumps and crashes above ground, the permanent lighting, the snores and grunts of other people, and the attentions of the little biting flies that seem to thrive in the warm, crowded shelters made sleep hard.

Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

Kyiv is entering its fourth winter following Russia's full-scale invasion

To the people who live here in Kyiv, it's frightening, certainly, if a drone or a missile hits close by, but enraging too. Over the years I've been in several cities that were being bombed by high-tech weaponry and the reaction always seems the same, whether it's Lebanon, Iraq, Serbia, or Ukraine: a combination of weariness and fury. In Kyiv the attacks come by night and day, making normal life almost impossible. An uninterrupted night's sleep is a rarity. The morning after the bridges were hit, people in the streets looked tired and worn.

Yet although they long for it to stop, there's no sign they want Ukraine to surrender. On the contrary, just about everyone I spoke to felt they had to keep fighting. That's borne out by an opinion poll last month by the KIIS organisation, a Ukrainian market research company, which found that 62% of people were prepared to put up with the war for as long as it took. Of those polled, 79% believed that Ukraine would win the war in the long run, and only 7% thought Russia would win. These aren't the reactions of a country which is being beaten to its knees.

Raving through the war

I don't have any doubt that Ukraine can survive the winter. Food is plentiful, though prices are high. Water is a problem, because the regular attacks on the power grid mean that it can't be pumped with any regularity. Kyiv underwent a large transformation under the Soviets, so there are large numbers of high-rise blocks of flats everywhere. Labouring up and down the stairs when there's no power is daunting, especially when you've got to carry quantities of water home.

We came across a small crowd of people in their 20s who had gathered outside a nightclub for a rave at three in the afternoon, because of the 11pm curfew. "It's a way of getting a bit of respite from everything," said one young woman. "It makes me feel I can put up with everything," said a man.

Do people still support President Volodymyr Zelensky? My team and I met an elderly woman wandering around Independence Square in the centre of Kyiv holding a photo of her son, who was missing on the Eastern front. She blamed Zelensky; if he didn't insist on carrying on the war, she believed, her son would still be alive. It isn't a response most people seem to share. The same polling organisation, KIIS, found that Zelensky's trust ratings hover around 54% to 57% — way below the 90% he was registering in the early days of the war in 2022, but not too bad for a man who's been in power now for more than seven years.

Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

Zelensky's ratings have dipped considerably

What comes across all the time in Kyiv is an absolute loathing of Russia. Putin reportedly launched his invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 because his intelligence chiefs assured him that Ukrainians longed to rejoin the Motherland.

Russian missiles have hit hospitals, clinics and schools. In many well-attested cases the Russians have used the "double-tap" method — sending in one missile, then waiting till the medics and rescuers gather before sending in another. At least 20,000 Ukrainian children have been abducted and taken to Russia, according to Ukraine's Ministry of Justice. In late March 2022, when the Ukrainians recaptured the satellite town of Bucha, on the outskirts of Kyiv, they found shocking evidence of torture and murder. Ukrainian soldiers call their Russian enemies Orcs, after the sub-human brutes in The Lord of the Rings. A country that has endured this kind of thing doesn't quickly forgive and forget. Russia denies that it targets civilians or civilian infrastructure.

Ukraine has never lost its own identity, even during the Soviet period. Some of Ukraine's culture was absorbed by Russia — "They call borsch [a famously delicious soup made of beetroot] theirs, but they got it from us," a waiter in a café here told me proudly. After the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Ukraine overwhelmingly voted for independence. The war has brought a fierce renewal of this desire to be completely separated from Russia.

It's not my usual beat, but my team and I went to film on the set of MasterChef Ukraine, currently one of the country's favourite television programmes. The studio was borrowed; the original one had been bombed. The executive producer had his phone in his hand the whole time, and was constantly glancing at it. The moment a red alert showed, it was his duty to shepherd everyone off the set to a nearby shelter. "People see our cuisine as a way of expressing their national identity," he said. It's one of the reasons the programme is so popular.

There are other ways in which people express their Ukrainian national identity under the bombs. There has been a boom for books being written and published about Ukraine and Ukrainian identity. Ukrainian and Russian are close as languages, though vocabulary and pronunciation differ. Nowadays the differences are emphasised. "Woe betide a writer who uses Russian spellings," a Ukrainian novelist told me.

How does it all end?

The war will end at some point; wars always do. But there has to be a clear winner before anyone backs down, and a lasting peace can be negotiated. US President Donald Trump and his advisers, people like Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, with their business backgrounds, have approached the situation as though it's a form of mergers and acquisitions: make a deal attractive enough, and the other side will accept it.

So, last week, Washington was rumoured to be offering a very Trumpian deal, that Ukraine should accept the loss of the land in the east which the Russians now control, and in return it was rumoured it could join Nato. It was a non-starter, because Russia would never accept it. The sweetener, in this US plan, was that the West's sanctions against Russia would be lifted, and both sides would benefit from unrestricted trading once again.

But neither side sees this as being about trade and profit. For Russia, it's about the dangers of being humiliated if it doesn't win. President Vladimir Putin has made it his personal war. By illegally taking Crimea from Ukraine in 2014, he made himself very popular in Russia. If he doesn't win this second stage of a 12-year campaign against Ukraine, the consequences for him personally could be disastrous. He's already had to face down one attempt against his rule: his former associate Yevgeny Prigozhin's march on Moscow in June 2023. In a much-quoted remark, reported last August, Putin is said to have confided to his associates that if he didn't win the war "they'll hang me". My sense is he's not concerned about trade with the West and the profit that will bring, so much as about his personal survival.

Similarly, Ukrainians aren't interested in the precise details that have leaked out of the various negotiations between the Americans and Russians. Their contempt for the US is immense; "they just failed us," said one Ukrainian I spoke to.

And they don't believe Russia will stick to any future peace agreement anyway. "They signed a treaty to accept our borders, and Putin broke it," a young man told me as he sat hunched over his laptop in a bookshop. "The only solution is to defeat them."

Image source, EPA

Image caption,

Tens of thousands of soldiers have died since the outbreak of war

Other people talked about the need to get huge reparations from Russia for the terrible destruction it has visited on their country. According to one estimate, reconstruction and recovery will cost more than $500bn (£383bn), an unthinkably huge amount for a country whose GDP was $200bn before the war. President Trump and his advisers don't seem to have addressed any of these issues in their negotiations.

Here in Kyiv, peace doesn't seem at all close. Russia's efforts to make life intolerable for Ukraine's citizens are certainly having a major effect. The war is often frightening for ordinary people, and it can be appallingly destructive of property and lives. But short of hugely escalating by attacking Ukraine with nuclear weapons, which is something China and the US are both thought to have warned him not to do, Putin can't seem to strike the knock-out blow against Ukraine that he needs.

At present it seems to people in Ukraine that the war will never come to an end. Yet it will, at some point: and then the crucial requirement will be to work out ways to stop Russia coming back for another round. One way would be if Ukraine joins Nato, but that's something Russia would only accept if it had been comprehensively defeated. Ukrainians might think that can happen, but most Western onlookers are more sceptical.

The daily and nightly sirens, the explosions of missiles and drones, the shortages and the fear and the darkness are all terrible. But they aren't enough to destroy Ukraine's will to continue fighting.
